precipitate

/prih-SIP-uh-tut/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Precipitate means done or acting with excessive haste and without proper thought — rash, sudden, and ill-considered.

The board's precipitate decision to launch the product before testing was finished ended in a costly recall.

Example

The mayor's precipitate decision to reopen the flooded road, announced before engineers had finished their inspection, had to be reversed the very next morning.

The decision was precipitate because it was made in a rush, before the necessary information was in. The bad outcome followed directly from that ill-considered haste — the mark of a precipitate action.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rash: Rash means acting without weighing the consequences — a rash promise, a rash purchase. It can describe anyone's snap decision, large or small. Precipitate is its formal, weightier cousin, reserved for serious actions taken in dangerous haste: a precipitate withdrawal, a precipitate resignation.

impulsive: Impulsive means driven by sudden urges rather than thought — an impulsive shopper buys on a surge of feeling. The push comes from inside, from emotion. A precipitate act is rushed rather than urged: taken too fast, before the facts are in, whatever the actor feels. Impulse is about mood; precipitate is about timing.

abrupt: Abrupt means sudden and without warning — an abrupt stop, an abrupt change of subject. It measures only suddenness and implies no blame. Precipitate always carries blame: the act was not just sudden but rushed ahead of proper thought, with consequences at stake. An abrupt decision may be wise; a precipitate one never is.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cautious: careful to avoid risk

measured: slow, calm, and considered

Where it sits · how much danger the rush invites — hasty → precipitate → reckless

hasty vs. precipitate: Hasty simply means too quick — a hasty breakfast harms no one. Precipitate is stronger: the rushed action is rash, and real consequences are on the line.

reckless vs. precipitate: Reckless goes beyond precipitate — not just rushing ahead of your own judgment, but charging forward with no regard for the danger at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before, forward, in advance (Latin prae-)

Root — cipit (from caput)

Root — cipit (from caput): head (Latin caput, capitis)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: adjective-forming ending (Latin -atus)

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin praeceps, 'headlong' — pre- (before, forward) + caput (head). A precipitate action is one you plunge into head-first, before your judgment can catch up with your feet.

Use the root in a new word: per capita

Use the root in a new word: per capita: Economists report a nation's income per capita — literally 'by heads,' meaning the amount per person.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Formal — two traps to avoid

As an adjective, precipitate is pronounced pri-SIP-uh-tut and describes rash actions and decisions: a precipitate withdrawal, a precipitate resignation. Don't confuse it with precipitous, which describes steepness ('a precipitous drop'). The related verb (pronounced pri-SIP-uh-tayt, 'to trigger suddenly') is a separate entry in this unit.
